title: -'s (Kate's camera / my brother's car etc.)
subtitle: Kate's camera / my parents' house / the roof of the building
summary: Use -'s to say that something belongs to a person, and of ... for things and places.

lesson.heading: Kate's camera
lesson.text: Kate holds a camera and says 'My camera'. So it is **Kate's** camera. A man stands next to his car and says 'My car'. It is **my brother's** car. On the door there is a sign: MANAGER. It is **the manager's** office. We normally use **-'s** for people.

examples.text: Paul is **a man's** name. Paula is **a woman's** name.

lesson.heading: -'s with no noun after it
lesson.text: You can use **-'s** on its own when the noun is already clear.

examples.text: 'Where were you last night?' 'I was at **Paul's**.'

left.label: my friend's house
left.text: One friend. We write **'s** after a singular word: friend, student, mother.
examples: my **friend's** house = his house or her house

right.label: my friends' house
right.text: Two or more friends. We write only **'** after a plural word: friends, students, parents.

lesson.heading: of ... for things and places
lesson.text: For things, places and ideas we do not use **-'s**. We use **of ...** instead.

examples.text: Look at the roof **of that building**.
We didn't see the beginning **of the film**.
Do you know the cause **of the problem**?

lesson.text: People take *-'s*: *my sister's house*. Things and places take *of*: *the end of the street*.

exercises.prompt: Sarah is married to Paul. Paul is ___ husband.
exercises.explanation: Sarah is a person, so we add -'s.

exercises.prompt: Helen and Brian have a son, James, and a daughter, Sarah. So James is ___ brother.
exercises.explanation: Sarah's brother = the brother of Sarah.

exercises.statement: What is the name of this village?
exercises.explanation: A village is a place, so we use of ... , not -'s.

exercises.statement: I stayed at the house of my sister.
exercises.explanation: I stayed at my sister's house. My sister is a person, so we use -'s.

exercises.prompt: Does the phrase talk about one person or about two or more people?

exercises.explanation: We can use -'s with no noun after it: my mother's = my mother's umbrella.

exercises.statement: Do you know the phone number of Simon?
exercises.explanation: Do you know Simon's phone number? Simon is a person, so we use -'s.

exercises.statement: Write your name at the top of the page.
exercises.explanation: A page is a thing, so we use of ... .

exercises.prompt: Sarah is James's sister, and she has a son, Daniel. So James is ___ uncle.
exercises.explanation: Daniel's uncle = the uncle of Daniel.

exercises.statement: The house of my parents isn't very big.
exercises.explanation: My parents' house isn't very big. Parents is plural, so we add only an apostrophe.
Spain is a place, so we use of ... .

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: Are you going to Silvia's party next week?
exercises.explanation: Silvia is a person, so we say Silvia's party, not the party of Silvia.
